column1: Starting on main, create and switch to a new feature branch with {{c1::git checkout -b feature/add-customer-email}}.
column2:
Make the database change on this branch rather than directly on main.
Review source

column1: Push committed changes on feature/add-customer-email to origin with {{c1::git push origin feature/add-customer-email}}.
column2:
Then open a pull request from that feature branch into main.
Review source

column1: A GitHub Actions workflow for proposed database changes normally uses the {{c1::pull_request}} event.
column2:
Configure the job to build the SQL database project.
Review source

column1: For pull_request events, branches: [main] filters the PR's {{c1::target branch}}.
column2:
It does not select feature branches by their source branch names.
Review source

column1: In Azure Repos, require a successful PR build through a {{c1::Build Validation}} branch policy.
column2:
Configure the build policy as Required on main to prevent ordinary PR completion when it fails.
Review source

column1: While on a feature branch, merge an up-to-date local main into it with {{c1::git merge main}}.
column2:
This integrates main into the current branch, not the current branch into main.
Review source

column1: In PowerShell, stage resolved conflicts in Tables\Customers.sql with {{c1::git add Tables\Customers.sql}}.
column2:
Staging records the resolved file but does not prove that the SQL schema is valid.
Review source

column1: After all merge conflicts are resolved and staged, finish the interrupted merge with {{c1::git merge --continue}}.
column2:
Run the SQL project build before completing the pull request.
